notes: “Plunder” follows the reading preserved in the Hebrew reading note; the written form differs.
The attack opens Moab’s flank. Verse 10 again names the Ammonites; the repeated name is retained rather than replaced with Moab.
vocabulary: People of the east
Groups living east of Ammon; the expression does not name one particular people.
Teman and Dedan
Places associated here with Edom and the reach of its devastation.

notes: The Hebrew gives the year and day but does not name the month.
A city’s “daughters” are its dependent settlements. The language of killing these daughters represents attacks on those communities.
The siege equipment is described with rare terms; the exact forms of the weapons are uncertain.
The pillars are monuments of the city’s strength; the wording does not identify them more precisely.
The Hebrew moves from a singular attacker to plural attackers. The shift is retained.
“Settled from the seas” renders a difficult expression that may describe the city’s seafaring population.

The final clause in the pinned Hebrew is positive: God will set splendor in the land of the living. Readings that make it another denial of Tyre’s return require a different understanding or alteration of the text.
vocabulary: Bare rock
The image connects the ruined city with a place for spreading fishing nets.
The pit
The realm of the dead, pictured below the land of the living.

notes: The wood names are approximate. The phrase rendered with cypress in verse 6 is especially difficult; its Hebrew words can be divided and understood differently.
The Gammadim are not otherwise identified here; the name is retained.
“Human lives” explicitly includes people among the traded goods.
Dedan and Aram follow the pinned Hebrew; other textual traditions differ. Pannag is an unidentified traded food or product.
“White wool” could instead involve a place name. The sequence Vedan, Javan, and Uzal in verse 19 is obscure, and the commercial route cannot be reconstructed confidently from it.
The description of textiles and their bindings is uncertain; the rendering follows a textile setting without claiming certainty about each item.
“Shorelands” in verse 28 is uncertain. The opening of verse 32 is difficult, as is the phrase describing Tyre as silenced in the sea.
vocabulary: Tyre
The trading city is addressed as a magnificent ship; its trading partners and crew become part of the ship’s story.
Ships of Tarshish
Large trading vessels associated with distant sea trade.

notes: The Hebrew writes Danel and supplies Daniel as its reading. The identity of the wise figure invoked in this taunt is disputed.
This lament is explicitly addressed to the king of Tyre. Its Eden and cherub imagery is retained without supplying another named character.
The gemstone names are approximate. The terms rendered as settings and mountings are difficult and can elsewhere name musical instruments.
The pinned pointing addresses the ruler as a guardian cherub. Another interpretation places him with a cherub. Verse 16 retains the divine speaker’s action and address to the cherub.
vocabulary: Heart of the seas
An image of Tyre’s offshore position and claimed security.
Cherub
A heavenly guardian figure, also associated with God’s throne elsewhere in Ezekiel.

notes: The claim can also be understood as “I made myself.” The Hebrew suffix leaves a consequential question about what Pharaoh claims to have made.

The final clause literally speaks of making every pair of loins stand. The awkward image of forcing backs upright is retained; readings such as making them stagger involve another interpretation or textual adjustment.
The forty years are retained as stated, without reducing them to a general expression for a long time.
This oracle’s twenty-seventh year is later than the surrounding dates. Its statement that Nebuchadnezzar received no payment from Tyre is retained.
vocabulary: Great sea creature
A formidable water creature used as an image of Pharaoh in the Nile; no particular species is certain.
Horn
An image of strength raised up for Israel; the concrete image is retained.

notes: Cub is not securely identified. “People of the covenant land” is also uncertain; the phrase does not explicitly identify the group.

The Egyptian place names follow familiar English forms: Memphis for Noph, Thebes for No, Pelusium for Sin, and On for Aven. Aven may also carry the sense of trouble or wickedness. Pi-beseth and Tahpanhes are retained.
The final expression about Memphis and daytime enemies is difficult; the draft preserves that image rather than supplying a reconstructed battle scene.
The feminine language can represent the cities or their people. A city’s daughters can refer to its dependent settlements.
vocabulary: Day of the LORD
A time of the LORD’s decisive action, described here as darkness and judgment upon nations.
Broken arm
An image of Pharaoh’s defeated military power.

notes: “Assyria” follows the pinned text. Some understand a tree name instead. The expression about the top among clouds can also be understood in relation to thick branches.
The address changes from “you” to “it” within the verse. The shift from Pharaoh to the tree image is retained.
The description of covering the deep and restraining its rivers is difficult. The mourning imagery is retained without reconstructing a physical event.
The tree’s “arm” represents those who supported its power.
vocabulary: Cedar
A towering tree becomes the image of imperial greatness and its fall.
Sheol
The realm of the dead, pictured as below the earth.

notes: The opening can be understood as likening Pharaoh to a lion or as a statement that he thought himself one. Another understanding takes the verb as being silenced. The following water-creature image remains explicit.
The term rendered as remains is rare and uncertain; the surrounding picture is of a carcass spread across the land.
No month is named in the pinned Hebrew date.

The pinned text says they do not lie with the fallen warriors and speaks of guilt on their bones. The draft preserves both difficulties rather than changing the verse into an unqualified honorable burial.
“My terror” follows the Hebrew reading note. The written form is “his terror.”
vocabulary: Daughters of nations
The nations are personified as women in the lament over their descent to the dead.
Uncircumcised
Here a recurring designation in the shame-filled picture of the slain among the dead.

notes: “Twelfth year” follows the pinned Hebrew. Other witnesses have a different year; the date has not been adjusted to resolve the chronology.
Eating “with the blood” may refer to consuming blood or to eating in connection with blood rites. The brief Hebrew expression is retained.
The language of love or desire in verse 31 leads into the comparison with a singer of love songs. Listening with pleasure is contrasted with acting on what is heard.
vocabulary: Watchman
A guard charged with seeing danger and sounding the alarm; the image explains Ezekiel’s responsibility to speak.
Pledge
Property held as security for a debt.

notes: “Fat” follows the pinned Hebrew pointing. A different pointing yields “milk.”
The pinned text says “destroy” concerning the fat and strong. Some witnesses instead speak of guarding them. The difficult judgment is retained.
The promised shepherd is called “my servant David.” The draft retains that name without supplying an explanation of his identity.
The planting is described with the Hebrew word for name or renown; some textual traditions instead connect it with peace.
vocabulary: Shepherds
An image for Israel’s leaders; the flock represents the people in their care.
Covenant of peace
A pledged relationship bringing safety and well-being to the people and their land.

sections.23: One shepherd and a covenant of peace

notes: The wording concerning hatred of bloodshed is difficult and stands within an oath. The pinned negative is retained rather than silently reversed.
The draft follows the reading note concerning the cities. The written form differs.
The relation between the rejoicing of the whole earth and Edom’s desolation can be read in more than one way. The draft takes the first as the setting for the second.
vocabulary: Mount Seir
The mountain region associated with Edom, addressed here as the people’s homeland.
Two nations and two lands
Israel and Judah, which Edom claims for itself.

notes: The phrase about pastureland and plunder is difficult; the draft retains the land-seizure setting without treating the exact wording as settled.
The reading notes affect the forms for the nations and, in verse 14, bereavement. Verse 15’s language of stumbling is kept distinct.
Menstrual impurity is a ritual category. The comparison does not say that menstruation itself is a moral offense.
The contrast is between stone and living flesh. “Flesh” here describes a responsive heart, not wrongdoing.
The willingness to be approached by Israel stands alongside earlier refusals to answer inquiry, including chapter 20.
vocabulary: Profane
To treat what is holy as common, here bringing dishonor upon God’s name among the nations.
Heart
In this setting, the center of a person’s intention and response, not only emotion.

notes: The Hebrew word ruach can mean spirit, breath, or wind. The movement among these senses connects the vision’s images; English uses different words where the immediate setting calls for them.
The bones belong to people described as slain. Verse 11 identifies the bones with the whole house of Israel; the explanation is part of the vision itself.
“Dwellings” follows the pinned text. Other readings understand the phrase in terms of backsliding or unfaithfulness.
The Hebrew places God’s dwelling “over them,” also understood as being among them.
vocabulary: Joseph and Ephraim
Names representing the northern tribes, contrasted with Judah and then joined with it.
David
The name used for the one shepherd and ruler of the reunited people.

notes: Rosh can be understood as “chief,” as in the draft, or as a proper name. The text does not provide a secure identification of Gog beyond the names given here.
“Navel of the earth” preserves the bodily image for a central place.
The Hebrew has “young lions,” an image associated with the merchants or their powerful associates. Some witnesses instead refer to villages.
The pinned Hebrew asks whether Gog will know. Other witnesses describe rousing or movement; the draft retains the question about knowing.
vocabulary: Gog
The named enemy addressed in chapters 38–39, associated with the land of Magog.
Unwalled settlements
Communities pictured as living securely without defensive walls, bars, or gates.

sections.10: A plan against a secure people

notes: The rare verb rendered as leading Gog on is uncertain. It does not clearly state that one-sixth of the army survives.
The Valley of the Travelers is not securely located. Hamon-gog means the multitude or horde of Gog.
The relation between the appointed workers and those passing through is difficult. Hamonah is a related place name meaning multitude.
The slaughtered warriors and rulers are described as sacrificial animals in an invitation to birds and wild animals. The disturbing comparison is retained.
The verb concerning shame and unfaithfulness is difficult. The draft takes it as bearing them; it has also been understood as forgetting them.
vocabulary: Cleanse the land
To remove the defilement associated here with unburied human remains.
Pour out my spirit
An image of God giving his spirit abundantly to Israel.

sections.17: A feast for birds and beasts
sections.21: The nations and Israel will know

notes: The measuring reed is six long cubits. Each long cubit is an ordinary cubit plus a handbreadth; exact modern equivalents would be approximate.
The repeated threshold in verse 6 and the differing vestibule measurements in verses 8–9 are retained. Their exact architectural relation is uncertain.
The sixty cubits are in the Hebrew, but the measured dimension is not specified clearly. The draft does not insert “high” or revise the number.
This verse’s vestibules and measurements are retained, despite questions about how they fit the other gate descriptions.
The Hebrew names jambs here, where related descriptions speak of vestibules. The difference is retained.
The fittings can be understood as hooks or ledges. A handbreadth is a small unit based on the breadth of a hand.
“Singers” and “east gate” follow the pinned Hebrew. Other witnesses and proposed readings have “two” rooms and a south gate.
The three cubits at either side are difficult to assign precisely. Verse 49 has eleven cubits, not twelve, and gives no number for the steps.
vocabulary: Beginning of the year
The date expression is retained without supplying a named month.
Threshold, jamb, vestibule
The lower entrance surface, upright side structure, and entrance porch or hall; exact arrangements in the vision are sometimes uncertain.

notes: “The width of the tent” is the pinned Hebrew’s unusual expression within this description of the temple building.
The entrance measurements are difficult to relate to one another; the six and seven cubits are both retained.
The draft understands the compact numerical phrase as three levels with thirty rooms on each. Other arrangements, including a total of thirty-three, have been proposed.
The word qualifying the cubit is rare. Its precise relation to the long cubit of 40:5 is uncertain.
Several architectural terms and the relations among the measurements are obscure. The draft follows the sequence of the Hebrew without claiming a fully resolved floor plan.
The source marks words concerning the wall of the main hall with extraordinary dots. The marked words are retained.
The objects being compared in verse 21 are uncertain. Verse 22 says “its length,” where some read “its base.” The wooden object is called both an altar and a table; its width is not supplied.
The wooden canopy or projecting structure is named with a rare word; its exact form is uncertain.
vocabulary: Most Holy Place
The innermost sacred space of the temple.
Cherubim
Plural of cherub. The carved figures here alternate with palm trees and are described with two faces.

notes: The Hebrew describes a one-cubit way. A reading of one hundred cubits appears in other textual traditions; the draft retains the pinned measurement.
“East” follows the pinned Hebrew. A southern position is often proposed to match the northern rooms.
The description of the corresponding wall and entrance is difficult; the draft does not present the layout as certain.

The reading note in verse 16 gives “five hundred.” Verses 16–19 explicitly measure in reeds, not cubits; verse 20 omits the unit. This large enclosure should not be silently harmonized with the five-hundred-cubit sanctuary plot in 45:2.
vocabulary: Most holy offerings
Offerings whose sacred status restricts where and by whom they may be eaten.
Holy and common
A distinction between what is set apart for sacred use and what is ordinary.

sections.13: The priests’ use of the rooms

notes: The pinned Hebrew says “when I came to destroy the city.” Other witnesses have “when he came.” The first-person wording is retained rather than silently corrected.
The phrase concerning the kings’ corpses and their high places is difficult. Some understand royal funerary monuments or read the final word as referring to their deaths.
The repeated references to the temple’s forms and regulations are retained.
The long cubit is again defined as a cubit plus a handbreadth. Some details of the altar’s base and ledges are uncertain; the stated numbers, square shapes, and four horns remain explicit.
Consecration is expressed with the image of filling hands, applied here to the altar. The Hebrew reading note supplies a plural form.
vocabulary: Footstool
The place for the soles of God’s feet, an image of his dwelling and rule.
Altar hearth
The upper surface where the offering burns; its Hebrew designation also contains a lion-like word form.

notes: The Hebrew shifts to “they broke my covenant” within the accusation against Israel. The change of subject is retained.
The restriction names uncircumcision of both heart and flesh. The bodily requirement and the inward image are both retained.
The repetition of the outer court is retained. The concern about making people holy through priestly garments belongs to the passage’s distinctions of sacred status.
The exceptions concerning a dead relative are specifically listed. The sister is further described as not having belonged to a husband.
The term for irrevocably devoted property can elsewhere involve destruction. Here the devoted thing is assigned to the priests, so the draft does not require its destruction.
vocabulary: Sons of Zadok
The priestly line given responsibility for service near the LORD in this vision.
Irrevocably devoted
Set apart under a binding dedication; the Hebrew term is herem.

notes: The large land dimensions omit their units, while verse 2 explicitly uses cubits. The draft leaves unsupplied units unstated. Verse 1 has ten thousand in the pinned Hebrew, where some witnesses have twenty thousand; verse 5 has twenty chambers, where some have cities.
The three stated amounts add to sixty shekels for a mina. The unusual formulation is retained.
A tenth of a bath from a cor is one-hundredth of the cor, since a cor contains ten baths. The stated proportions are retained.
The pinned Hebrew says the seventh day of the month. Another textual tradition gives a different date in the seventh month.
The compact phrase describing the festival is understood here as a festival of seven days. It does not introduce a separate Feast of Weeks into the Passover instruction.
vocabulary: Ephah, bath, homer
Measures for grain and liquid: an ephah and a bath each equal one-tenth of a homer.
Shekel, gerah, mina
Weight units. The verse specifies twenty gerahs to a shekel and amounts totaling sixty shekels to a mina.

notes: This is the inner court’s east gate. The closed outer east gate in 44:1–2 is a different gate.
The daily offering described here is a morning offering. An evening offering is not added to the text.
The year of release marks the return of a grant made to a servant. This passage does not state the number of years in the cycle.

The word describing the corner courts is uncertain and has been understood as enclosed, open, or related to smoke. The source also marks a word about the corner courts with extraordinary dots; it is retained.
vocabulary: Year of release
The appointed year when a servant’s grant from the prince returns to the prince’s property.
Guilt offering
An offering associated with liability and reparation; its preparation is restricted to the priestly area here.

notes: The water is described as healed. The unnamed sea is commonly understood as the Dead Sea, but the draft retains “sea.” Marshes and swamps are explicitly excepted from the healing.
The Hebrew form for the streams is dual. The draft retains the plural image without supplying a map of separate branches.
Joseph’s portions are understood as two, corresponding to the two tribal allotments named for his descendants in chapter 48.
“Measure” in verse 18 follows the pinned Hebrew; another reading names Tamar. The Wadi in verse 19 is not explicitly named in this verse.
Resident foreigners with families among Israel receive an inheritance in the tribe where they live. That entitlement is explicit in the passage.
vocabulary: Arabah
The rift-valley region toward which the water flows eastward.
Wadi
A stream channel that may be dry for part of the year.

notes: Many large dimensions again omit a unit. The draft preserves the stated numbers without supplying cubits or reeds where the text does not name them.
The Hebrew reading note omits an extra written “five.” The four sides are each four thousand five hundred in the reading followed here.
The eighteen thousand measures the city’s perimeter. “The LORD Is There” renders the name given to the city.
vocabulary: Contribution
Land set apart from the tribal allotments for the sanctuary, priests, Levites, city, and associated uses.
Tribal gates
The city’s twelve gates carry the names of Israel’s tribes, connecting the city’s layout with the people.
